awd_titl_txt: STTR Phase I:  A platform to overcome immunodominance in vaccine development
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) Phase I project is to advance a novel vaccine platform to develop engineered vaccines that provide longer lasting protection against infectious diseases. Several current vaccines face challenges in reliably protecting populations against rapidly evolving pathogens where prior exposure negatively impacts vaccine effectiveness. This project develops an innovative approach aimed at boosting the immune response to critical parts of pathogens, overcoming limitations associated with previous exposures or immune system biases. By directing immune responses toward conserved, essential regions of pathogens, the innovation has significant commercial and societal potential, including the development of vaccines that are effective across multiple pathogen variants. As an initial area of translation, the technology will be applied toward prevention of healthcare-associated infections caused by antibiotic-resistant bacteria. This approach addresses an unmet clinical need and offers healthcare systems substantial cost savings and improved patient outcomes. The market opportunity for such vaccines is substantial, with potential annual revenues exceeding $200 million by the third year of commercial production. The resulting technology and its applications could provide durable competitive advantages through enhanced vaccine effectiveness, positioning it as a key factor in enabling commercial success and improving public health.

This Small Business Technology Transfer (STTR) Phase I project aims to overcome a significant limitation in vaccine development known as immune imprinting, which occurs when prior exposure to pathogens biases immune responses away from protective targets. The objective is to utilize a novel method involving engineered antigens containing chemically modified amino acids to enhance immune recognition and stimulate targeted protective responses. The research goals are to validate computational methods for accurately predicting optimal sites for antigen modifications, demonstrate increased antibody production specifically targeting essential pathogen regions, and confirm that these improvements enhance cross-strain protection. Research activities will include computational modeling to predict antigen modification sites, genetic engineering techniques to produce modified vaccine candidates, and immunological studies in animal models to evaluate effectiveness. Anticipated technical outcomes include validated predictive tools that significantly reduce experimental trial-and-error, proof-of-concept demonstration of enhanced antibody responses toward targeted regions of antigens, and improved vaccine induced protection in animal models.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Vaccines are one of the most effective tools available to prevent infectious diseases. However, for several diseases of significant concern to public health, vaccines are limited by poor recognition by the immune system by certain vaccine antigens, which inhibits the rate and durability of immune response. To address this challenge, Nitro Biosciences is advancing a technology that enables precise modifications to vaccine antigens to create new regions recognized by the immune system, with the goal of improving the strength, breadth, and duration of protection. Through support from the National Science Foundation, this project sought to develop the technology into a broadly applicable platform for engineering next-generation vaccines.

Over the course of this project, we successfully developed and validated a screening platform to identify engineered proteins with the potential to stimulate novel T cell responses. This approach enables researchers to evaluate libraries of different engineered proteins simultaneously, significantly expanding the number of candidates that can be investigated during vaccine discovery. We applied this technology to engineer vaccine antigens related to a bacterial pathogen responsible for significant gastrointestinal disease. In these studies, we demonstrated the successful production of large libraries of engineered antigens and identified modifications that created new regions recognized by the immune system. Importantly, through in vivo studies, we confirmed that these engineered proteins could stimulate cellular responses that were not observed with unmodified proteins, demonstrating that the platform can be used to design novel antigens and engineer variants capable of stimulating new immune responses.

The outcomes of this project advance our understanding of how targeted modifications to proteins can influence immune recognition and provide new tools for investigating the development of vaccines and immune-based therapies. In addition, the project identified important biological and technical factors that influence the effectiveness of this approach, providing valuable guidance for future research and development. These findings establish a foundation for further exploration of engineered proteins, non-canonical amino acid modifications, and improved screening strategies for vaccine development. More broadly, the technologies and knowledge developed through this NSF-supported research have potential applications in biological research, infectious disease prevention, cancer immunotherapy, and animal health, contributing to ongoing efforts to develop more effective and precisely targeted immune-based treatments.
